content_preview.title: UC Irvine-Led Team Revises Nearby Exoplanet GJ 3378b to a Lighter, More Earth-Like Mass Inside the Habitable Zone
content_preview.summary: A UC Irvine-led study cut GJ 3378b's estimated mass and orbital period, placing the nearby super-Earth more solidly within its star's habitable zone.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A team led by astronomers at the University of California, Irvine has substantially revised the mass and orbit of a nearby exoplanet first identified in 2024, finding it is lighter, closer to its star, and more likely to be a rocky, Earth-like world than originally measured. The planet, GJ 3378b, orbits a red dwarf star about 25 light-years from Earth in the constellation Camelopardalis, according to [UC Irvine News](https://news.uci.edu/2026/06/30/uc-irvine-astronomers-discover-a-n...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (958 words, within the 400-1200 range) using the standard Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis format. Clear, precise science writing appropriate to the subject; no padding or sensationalism.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 4 sources personally verified, 2 via committed snapshots and 2 via manual fallback after automated snapshotting failed. (1) news.uci.edu — automated fetch timed out at 15s (script threshold) and a WebFetch retry hit a 504. The site is not dead: a direct curl with a browser user-agent returned HTTP 200 with full content after ~30s (the page is simply slow to render), and I read the full press release text. It verbatim-confirms both Robertson quotes ('This one's exciting...', 'This super-Earth gets about 90 percent...', the apple-atmosphere analogy) and the Gogod James quote, plus the Habitable Worlds Observatory/2040s detail, the funding-source names, and the co-author list (Endl, Cochran, Stefansson, Mahadevan). One minor attribution nuance: the article's opening sentence bundles 'red dwarf' and 'constellation Camelopardalis' under the UC Irvine News citation, but those two specific descriptors are not in the UCI press release itself — they are, however, independently confirmed by both Space.com ('faint red dwarf star in the constellation of Camelopardalis') and Sci.News ('red dwarf star located 25 light-years away in the northern constellation of Camelopardalis'), both of which are cited elsewhere in the same article. The underlying fact is true and multiply-sourced within the piece; this is a citation-bundling nuance, not a factual error, so I did not file a corrections record for it. (2) sci.news — snapshot read from disk (source-1.html.gz, sha256 verified against manifest); confirms mass/period figures, the Endl quote verbatim, and the cosmic-shoreline framing. (3) space.com — snapshot read from disk (source-2.html.gz, sha256 verified); confirms the original 5.26-Earth-mass/mini-Neptune figure with the exact quoted phrase 'putting it in mini-Neptune territory of being a larger, mostly gaseous world,' the radial-velocity/Doppler-wobble detection method description, the JWST/TRAPPIST-1 transit-spectroscopy contrast, and the Endl 'ultimate goal is biosignatures' quote verbatim. (4) doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae732b — the snapshot (source-3.html.gz, sha256 verified) captured a Radware Bot Manager captcha page from validate.perfdrive.com, not the paper; the publisher (IOPscience) also returned HTTP 403 to a direct WebFetch retry. I located the same paper's arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.16499, identical title 'A Revised Mass and Period for the Habitable Zone super-Earth GJ 3378b: A Planet Straddling the Cosmic Shoreline') and confirmed via its abstract/HTML: revised minimum mass 2.3 ± 0.4 Earth masses and orbital period 21.45 ± 0.01 days (exact match to the article); the verbatim phrases 'increases the likelihood that the planet has a terrestrial composition' and 'remains within the conservative circumstellar liquid-water habitable zone' (exact match); the HPF+NEID+CARMENES+SPIRou instrument combination (exact match); and the full 21-author list including Robertson, Endl, Cochran, Stefansson, and Mahadevan (article's 'among its authors' framing is accurate). I additionally traced the original 2024 discovery paper (Moutou et al., A&A, arXiv:2406.10384) and confirmed the lead author is indeed 'C. Moutou' and the original figures are minimum mass 5.26 (+0.94/-0.97) Earth masses and orbital period 24.728 (+0.054/-0.058) days — the article's '24.73 ± 0.06 days' is a reasonable symmetric rounding of that asymmetric uncertainty. Every direct quote in the submission is verbatim against its cited source; every specific number traces to a source I personally read.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinations, fabrications, or unsupported specifics found. Headline, summary, and lead are all backed by the verified sources. The two automated 'unreachable source' findings were snapshot-tooling artifacts (slow site, publisher bot-wall), not content problems — both were resolved through direct verification.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no editorializing, no AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ and src/content/article-meta/ for prior GJ 3378b / Gliese 3378 / exoplanet coverage; found none. This is a genuinely new topic — no duplicate or substantial overlap with recently published articles. No sufficiently specific editorial link to existing coverage was found to warrant a curated related_articles entry.
concerns: Minor citation-bundling nuance in the lead sentence (see source_verification) — the 'red dwarf'/'Camelopardalis' descriptors are attributed to UC Irvine News but are only explicit in the Space.com and Sci.News snapshots, both cited elsewhere in the article. True and multiply-sourced within the piece; not treated as a corrections-worthy error.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Exceptionally well-sourced submission. All four sources were personally read (two via committed snapshots, two via manual fallback after automated snapshot capture failed for infrastructure reasons unrelated to source validity). Every quote, name, and figure — including precise before/after mass and orbital-period values traced back to both the 2024 discovery paper and the 2026 revision paper — checks out exactly. Approved without corrections.
